scope: Whole current restored Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut/Q660692: all three colonnaded terraces and intrinsic open courts, two central stone ramps/steps/masonry rails, square-pier porticos/upper Osirian pilasters, attached Hathor/Anubis chapels and upper solar-cult/sanctuary wall complexes. Native individual architecture/column footprints control physical parts. Site1079542368 is only archaeological context boundary, not a filled building extrusion. era: Enduring restored temple exterior shell represented by clear creator2010/2016 exteriors and current individual native architectural controls. originalReview.notes: Full2010 whole-temple front oblique: three stacked stone colonnades/central rising ramps, broad central terrace and flanking retaining walls, upper row Osirian piers. Natural cliff, visitor facilities, people/vehicles excluded.

2010 lower ramp looking outward/down: actual paving/intrinsic flanking masonry ramp rails and lower court enclosure relationship. Ground courtyard mainly sand; not a new broad concrete slab or copied landscape.

2010 upper/middle portico detail: real open paired rows of square stone piers/architraves/roof slab and pale limestone masonry, upper Osirian pilasters and deep shaded colonnade. No copied relief/people/interior objects.

2010 upper ramp looking down across actual middle terrace/courtyard: central stone ramp/stepped lane/flanking masonry, broad paved middle platform and intrinsic rubble perimeter. Adjacent separate temple/landscape excluded.

2016 whole front from middle terrace: stacked middle/upper colonnades, central ramp/steps/rails, warm pale stone/pylonic parapet and upper Osirian pilasters; construction scaffold and free-standing sphinx/furniture excluded.

candidates.filename: Anubis Chapel, Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut, Luxor, LG, EGY (48010599421) (Thoth and Amun).jpg
candidates.caption: This is the Mortuary Temple of Queen Hatshepsut, designed by Senenmut, and located outside of Luxor (site of the ancient Egyptian capital of Thebes) in Upper Egypt.  Constructed during the reign of Queen Hatshepsut during the 18th Dynasty of the Ancient Egyptian New Kingdom between 1478 and 1458 BC.  The temple complex was dedicated to the god Amun and Hatshepsut, and has three levels, and is aligned so that sunlight reaches the innermost chamber of the complex during the Winter Solstice sunrise each year.  The structure is home to Hatshepsut’s burial chamber, a suncourt on the top level, three colonnades, and a chapel dedicated to Anubis, the Egyptian god of death, mummification, and embalming.  The structure is considered to be the closest the Ancient Egyptians came to building Classical-style architecture like that of Rome and Greece.  The structure contains many intact carvings and painted reliefs within, while the mortuary temple of Mentuhotep II sits in ruins nearby, having served as the inspiration and as a source of materials for the structure.  The structure fell into disuse after Hatshepsut’s death in 1458BC, and eventually fell into ruins, with the lowermost level being partially buried by sand and debris that accumulated over almost 3400 years, while the uppermost level’s colonnade collapsed.  In 1895, the ruins began to be excavated, and, over the course of about a century, the structure was partially restored by reconstituting the fallen stones and pieces back to their original locations, with the Polish Academy of Sciences in Warsaw being responsible for much of the work.

candidates.filename: Templo funerario de Hatshepsut, Luxor, Egipto, 2022-04-03, DD 13.jpg
candidates.caption: Aerial view during sunrise of the Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut, Luxor, Egypt. The mortuary temple built during the reign of Pharaoh Hatshepsut of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. The temple is considered to be a masterpiece of ancient architecture. Its three massive terraces rise above the desert floor and into the cliffs of Deir el-Bahari. Her tomb, KV20, lies inside the same massif capped by El Qurn, a pyramid for her mortuary complex. Across the river Nile, the whole structure points towards the monumental Eighth Pylon, Hatshepsut's most recognizable addition to the Temple of Karnak and the site from which the procession of the Beautiful Festival of the Valley departed.
candidates.sourceFamily: commons:Templo funerario de Hatshepsut, Luxor, Egipto, 2022-04-03, DD 13.jpg
